body.text: Will the Australian parliament ever debate AUKUS? The latest opportunity came up in April this year, when the Albanese government released its latest National Defence Strategy; its text is yet to be debated in parliament. The opposition’s criticism of government defence policy has been limited to arguing overall spending must increase to 3 per cent of GDP if the costs of AUKUS (which it supports) aren’t to reduce or delay expenditure on other weapons and programs.

But federal MPs have not been entirely silent on AUKUS. In debating the bills establishing a pathway for AUKUS, parliamentarians have said much in favour of AUKUS and not much against. Indeed, the purpose of one law — this year’s Defence Amendment (Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence) Act — is to limit the circulation of information about defence policy to MPs who support AUKUS.

The passage of these bills has demonstrated one effect of bipartisan agreement: it gives the government cover to tighten its grip on the legislature as a whole. In this sense, AUKUS is not just a defence policy; it is a recasting of democratic process.

Concretely, AUKUS is an agreement among three nation-states to share technology of military significance. This includes, but is not limited to, submarines propelled by nuclear reactors. Whether Australia will ever own a conventionally armed nuclear-powered submarine, or SSN, secondhand or new, remains an open question, but Australia will undoubtedly be responsible for resourcing US vessels of this kind at a port just south of Perth.

Some MPs exult in the distinction this task will confer on Australia. “Suddenly,” declared Liberal MP James Stevens, “we have such a preferential status, as an ally of the United States and the United Kingdom, to partner with them and acquire their great capability.”

That capability includes knowing how to build, operate and maintain vessels with nuclear reactors inside them. Because the people with the necessary knowledge will be not only members of Australia’s armed forces but in many cases employees of private firms, the government amended security legislation to enabling vetting employees of “industrial partners” — in other words, employees not in the Australian Defence Force.

In debate, the opposition’s Andrew Wallace estimated this amendment would give rise to 30,000 applications for security clearance each year. Labor’s Matt Thistlethwaite estimated, more conservatively, that AUKUS would create 20,000 jobs “over the coming decades.” Whatever the figure, all these workers will have to pass a security test, and so the efficiency of the Australian Government Security Vetting Agency will become a concern. The amendment also enables ASIO and other agencies to exchange information about individuals and introduces a new framework for reviewing ASIO security assessments and clearance decisions.
Speaking in support of the bill on 15 June 2023, Liberal MP Keith Wolahan marvelled at Australia’s talent for secret dealing:

What Wolahan considered virtuous and clever, others see as a lapse in global citizenship. As the Parliamentary Library reported in mid 2023, “some states and arms control experts,” including Tariq Rauf, a former head of verification and security policy coordination with the International Atomic Energy Agency, or IAEA, feel the three AUKUS states (and the IAEA secretariat) have been “less than transparent” in their presentation of the nuclear submarine agreement to the IAEA’s board of governors, and to IAEA member states for approval.

Views like these are less important to both government and opposition MPs than winning AUKUS partners’ trust. “This is the first time since the 1950s that the US has shared its crown jewel technology — that is, nuclear propelled submarines — with another country,” Wallace reminded the House in March 2024. “The only other time it has done that was in the 1950s, and it was with the United Kingdom.”

The government believes Australia has a good record of managing nuclear waste and is confident this will continue if it eventually owns nuclear-powered submarines. The AUKUS parties agreed to adhere to IAEA safeguards for storing dismantled reactors, high-level radioactive waste and spent nuclear fuel — the refuse that would arrive in the 2050s according to the AUKUS schedule.

During debate on new AUKUS-related nuclear-safety legislation in May 2023, opposition MPs pointed to the one major difference between the government and the opposition. If the proposed regulatory framework was good enough to deal with waste from submarines, opposition speakers argued, then it was good enough to manage waste from a civil nuclear program. Nuclear reactors should propel not only submarines but also businesses and households.

In the minds of opposition MPs — at least at the time — defence and energy policy are linked by the need for a nuclear-capable workforce. In May 2023 shadow defence minister Luke Howarth quantified them: “200 subject matter experts in Australia to make top-level decisions regarding the eight new SSN-AUKUS subs, with at least twenty years’ experience in nuclear technology each”; “senior scientists, electrical and mechanical engineers, technical managers, reactor operators and even health physicists”; and “4000-plus workers… trained up in nuclear awareness to help to maintain the AUKUS submarines.”
Australia risked failing to build the workforce AUKUS requires, Howarth argued, because the Greens and Labor were beholden to anti-nuclear sentiment.

Shadow climate change and energy minister Ted O’Brien predicted Australia would be the only operator of nuclear-propelled submarines not also using nuclear reactors to generate electricity for civil use. The synergy of civil and military commitments to nuclear reactors was necessary, O’Brien argued, for Australia to develop the nuclear-savvy workforce AUKUS requires. Since the 2025 election the Coalition parties have muffled their advocacy of nuclear power: they are now, they say, “technology agnostic.”

The Greens didn’t disagree with the opposition’s linking of civil and military uses of nuclear energy, but they deplored both. In their circulated amendment to the government’s bill they made two claims: that Indigenous Australians were especially vulnerable to “every facet of the nuclear industry” and that the bill “is the first step in the largest nuclear program in Australian history, which is strongly opposed by millions of Australians, the peace and environment movements and a broad range of unions.” The opposition and the government combined to defeat the Greens’ amendment.

Another piece of legislation, the Defence Amendment (Safeguarding Australia’s Military Secrets) Act 2024, recognised a global market exists for those equipped with the knowledge to make, operate and maintain the sophisticated technologies used for military purposes. While it is possible to focus on what this law forbids (unapproved working beyond Australia attracts a severe penalty), this Act is better seen as enabling Australians to work in a wider labour market. Former defence staff members and other individuals who wish to work for, or provide specified training to, foreign military organisations or government bodies will be allowed to do so, as long as these foreign powers are approved by the Australian government.

Associated legislation facilitates collaboration, co-development, and innovation among the AUKUS partners by exempting Britain and the United States from most export permit requirements for military and dual-use goods and technology.

Labor’s Peter Khalil explained in March 2024 that the government aimed to establish “seamless technological transfers with our AUKUS partners” not only skilled employees with security clearances and permission to work for governments or companies, but also military assets bought and sold within what Khalil and the defence department refer to as an “export-licence-free environment between AUKUS partners.” Shadow defence minister Philip Thompson referred to an “export licence treaty environment, which will support industry, education and research sectors in all three nations,” opening “further opportunities for small and medium enterprises in Australia.”

Speakers supporting the Albanese government’s AUKUS-enabling laws acknowledged they were responding to the expectations of the two AUKUS partners. Khalil referred in March 2024 to “a standard of controls comparable to those of the United States to access the national exemption from US export control licensing requirements under the US Arms Export Control Act.” Wallace urged Australia not to be “the laggard.” The US National Defense Authorization Act, he said, “requires the US Congress, with the certification of the US president, to be satisfied with Australia’s progress in implementing security and export frameworks within 120 days of the NDAA’s enactment. The first certification date is 20 April 2024. That is in less than one month.”

Deadlines set by AUKUS partners left little time for the Senate Standing Committee on Defence, Foreign Affairs and Trade to review the Defence Trade Controls Amendment bill. Rapid as this review was (December 2023–January 2024), it did allow some senators to point to risks imposed on Australia’s technology and research sector by AUKUS’s obligations.

The Greens’ dissenting report highlighted the risk it posed to scientific work in which collaborators come from a variety of countries. They cited semiconductor industry fears that the law would make recruiting and retaining skilled labour from overseas more difficult. Non-Labor senators referred to “concern from the Australian Defence industry small and medium enterprise (SME) sector at what they regard as an increased administrative burden, increased criminal penalties for non-compliance — despite best efforts at compliance — and the potential to limit exports to countries outside of the AUKUS partnership.”

During debate on the bill in March 2024, independent MP Zoe Daniel echoed these fears. “Australian companies will have to sign up to incredibly rigid restrictions and then hope the Americans give them the contracts,” she said, adding that “even with these new provisions in place” Australia’s defence department is more happy buying from overseas, “and the US in particular,” than encouraging a sovereign Australian defence capability. Australia would become “even more dependent on the US defence sector, which is notoriously inward-looking and subject to the parochial demands of individual members of Congress.”

The Greens wanted the bill rejected entirely. Stephen Bates, like Daniel, cited the concerns of universities and advanced technology companies working with researchers in South Korea or India, for example, on dual-use technology. They “would have to stop and get approval from the minister or risk ten years’ imprisonment,” he argued, adding: “This bill risks creating a significant disincentive for most of the world to work with Australian researchers and to trade critical technology.”
Nonetheless, the bill became law.

Parliamentary comment on AUKUS’s strategic benefit to Australia has been rare. Do MPs think the benefit is so obvious there’s no need to spell it out, or do they lack the confidence to talk about military strategy? An exception is former army officer Luke Gosling, a Labor MP who co-founded the Parliamentary Friends of AUKUS. On 11 September 2024 (an anniversary prompting rumination on security), he explained how the nuclear-propelled submarines’ “almost unlimited range” would affect “any adversary’s mind.” The submarines’ importance would be clear if an enemy attempted

to sever our sea lines of communication or blockade our ports… or if they try to encircle us strategically and project force against us through our northern approaches or sever our connections…Their ships would be vulnerable to being sunk while they staged any assault or attempt to cut us off. Their submarines would be liable to being stalked and destroyed by the best submariners in the world.

Some of the friends of AUKUS believe Australia will never have to take aggressive action because the weapons endowed by AUKUS “are not built to fight a certain war; they’re built to prevent future war,” in the words of Keith Wolahan on 11 September 2024. “Our task is to make sure that potential aggressors in the globe wake up and say, ‘Not today.’ One of the reasons they’ll say ‘Not today’ is AUKUS.”

For AUKUS to deter anyone from blockading Australia, however, what matters is how “the adversary” sees the United States. Former senior defence official Hugh White argues in his recently published book Hard New World: Australia’s Post-American Future that China’s appraisal of the United States probably differs from the Australian political elite’s. China, he argues, has good reason to doubt the US would project force in the ways imagined by Gosling because Washington, having assessed China’s strength, no longer thinks it can prevail militarily over China in the western Pacific. The AUKUS agreement doesn’t oblige the US or Britain to defend Australia.

Merely possessing lethal weapons is not enough: for the nuclear-propelled subs to be a deterrent, China would have to believe the US will use them to protect Australia. For many in parliament it is an article of faith that the Americans will repeat what they did in the Battle of the Coral Sea. That we “share values” with the US (surely a debatable proposition) substitutes for debate about the US’s interests and its willingness to suffer.

For Barnaby Joyce, also speaking on 11 September 2024, using AUKUS to augment Australian fire power is urgent, because China is already encircling Australia. “Do we honestly believe, when Wang Yi [China’s foreign minister] is going to Timor-Leste, Papua New Guinea, Kiribati, the Solomons, Vanuatu and Fiji, and having discussions with the Cook Islands, that this is by chance? These are tactics against Australia — it always is. It’s encirclement. You don’t have to invade Australia; you just have to cut it off. If you cut it off, you win.”
Claiming underspending on Australia’s Navy, he remarked that “we have a formidable gap to fill… and AUKUS is fundamental in that process.”

With Labor, Liberal and National Party MPS united in support of every bill that enables AUKUS and (evidently) sharing an unquestioning belief the US would fight any adversary menacing Australia, only the Greens and independents have expressed doubts about AUKUS.

The Greens were particularly provoked by last year’s Defence Housing Australia Amendment Bill. According to Labor senator Ellie Whiteaker, a supporter of the bill, the law would commit the Australian government to provide housing for personnel implementing not only AUKUS “but also the US Force Posture Initiatives, the Australia–Japan Reciprocal Access Agreement and the Australia–Singapore Military Training Initiative.”

Why was the government not equally committed to housing Australians who aren’t involved in defence, asked Greens senator David Shoebridge in August 2025. The government will “build homes for pretty much anybody in the war industry, while they’re resisting the repeated calls the Greens have made to build homes for Australians who desperately need them.” Observed senator Barbara Pocock, “When the US asks, suddenly it’s not impossible for governments to build houses anymore, this time for non-Australians [namely] foreign military organisations, foreign governments and foreign military contractors and subcontractors.”

To give priority to Aussies over foreigners has plenty of rhetorical appeal, but whether the Greens have an alternative defence policy is another matter. Shoebridge sees risks in hosting submarines at HMAS Stirling (aka Submarine Rotational Force West), near Perth: “Even US defence hawks point out that, once that base is up and running, it will be a high-priority target in any conflict between the US and any other peer power.” He believes that “we live in one of the most secure parts of the planet, secure from these geopolitical conflicts that the US wants to get us involved in, and, far from using our geography to protect ourselves, the Coalition and Labor are inviting us into the next US war.”

The Greens want Australia to repudiate AUKUS and revise the ANZUS treaty. Shoebridge’s press release responding to the Albanese government’s National Defence Strategy called for “a genuinely sovereign defence force that would protect us here at home.” What weapons and programs would the Greens support? Without answering such questions, the Greens don’t have a credible alternative to AUKUS.

In February this year Shoebridge admitted he finds such questions distasteful. Discussing a proposed new parliamentary defence policy committee, he urged that it include at least one person who would question the views of those who he referred to as the “war parties.” “They will still be patting each other on the back,” he added, “thinking about which mate to give a contract to and working out how much they can bow and grovel to Donald Trump. They will still be the majority of the committee. But at least there might be one voice in there testing them — I hope it won’t be me….”

That parliament needs such a committee was universally acknowledged by MPs, but different parties had different views about its composition. Labor and the opposition were united in believing that dissenters shouldn’t be welcome in its ranks.

“Committees dealing with sensitive national security matters require trust — trust between members, trust with Defence and the intelligence community and, most importantly, trust with our allies,” declared the Coalition’s Michaelia Cash. “Appointing Greens or independents would politicise classified defence matters, undermine that trust and weaken the purpose of the committee.”

Cash’s colleague Dave Sharma conceded that MPs “are entitled to have a legitimately different point of view,” but he feared that those “who do not, basically, share the strategic assessment that underpins the scale-up in the defence forces” would pose a threat to the committee’s functioning. “I don’t think we can risk having political games being played or classified information being misused.”

Liberal senator Jessica Collins agreed: “Those who are unwilling to hold the sovereignty of this nation above all else and who would seek to use this platform to defund and hamstring our defence forces are unwelcome.”

The Nationals’ Michael McCormack drew the line more explicitly. Greens and crossbenchers “do not share the same values for our military, and oversight thereof, that Labor, Liberal and National members of parliament and senators would have.” He welcomed what he understood to be Richard Marles’s assurance “that committee members must, firstly, support the Australian Defence Force and increased resourcing for defence. That’s absolutely bottom line. And, secondly, they must support AUKUS.” Marles’s assurances about who would be barred from the defence committee were a condition of National Party support, McCormack added.

That Cash, Sharma, Collins and McCormack could refer so confidently to a line dividing trusted MPs from those not trusted reflects the intensity of polarisation AUKUS has brought to parliament, exacerbated more recently by differences in responding to the Trump administration and the Hamas–Israel clash. In the four years since Labor bought into AUKUS, the pro-AUKUS bloc in the parliament — that is, Labor, Liberal, Nationals and One Nation — has become openly contemptuous of MPs who question AUKUS, the Trump administration and Israel’s response to Hamas’s October 2023 attack.

For example, on 11 September 2024, Andrew Wallace — after expressing opposition warmth for Marles — said that while he hoped the Liberals would replace Labor as the governing party, he would be consoled by Labor winning the next election in its own right “because the worst thing that could ever happen to this place, to this country, is you guys ever being in a power-sharing arrangement with the Greens. God help us. God help this country if the Greens are ever sharing power with the Labor Party again.”

Albanese’s victory in 2025 put that fear to rest. In the second Albanese government, solidarity between Labor, Liberal and the Nationals has hardened into a pact of scorn for Greens and independent MPs.

Four attempts were made to amend the Defence Amendment (Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence) Bill, each seeking to determine the composition of the defence committee. McCormack wanted the law to limit committee membership to the opposition and the government parties of the day: no teals or Greens. He treated the House to these observations about the Greens:

They want to change all things military. They don’t believe in even the executive having the authority to send people into war. If it were up to the Greens… if trouble started, they would want parliament recalled. They would want to get their travel entitlements. They’d want to have sit-down lunches and discussions and Senate inquiries and go backwards and forwards. And, in the meantime, the country would probably be invaded. You just can’t rely on them.
The government voted McCormack’s amendment down 97–35.

Independent MP Nicolette Boele (with support from Andrew Gee, another independent) proposed the committee include two members from among small parties or independents. Her amendment was defeated 98–10.

In the Senate, One Nation proposed a place on the defence committee for at least one representative from each minor party, naming them as One Nation, the Nationals and the Greens. The senators voted 28–13 against the amendment. Senator Shoebridge proposed the committee include one senator and one lower house member who is a member neither of the government nor of the opposition. This was defeated 26–12.

The Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence has commenced work. At its first meeting on 12 May, the committee elected Labor senator Deborah O’Neill as chair and Liberal senator Dave Sharma as deputy, with eight other members: Labor’s Matt Burnell, Tony Zappia, Ellie Whiteaker, Susan Templeman, Meryl Swanson and Zaneta Mascarenhas, the Liberal National Party of Queensland’s Andrew Wallace and Phillip Thompson, and the Liberals’ James Paterson.

“We are asked to accept an awful lot about AUKUS as an act of faith,” Zoe Daniel observed in March 2024. For the pro-AUKUS bloc to denounce the apostate MPs and exclude them from the defence committee enacts that faith, but will it assure Australians’ faith in the major parties’ judgment? “Transparency and accountability are among the keys to voter confidence in public policy,” Daniel suggested on 11 September 2024. “If ever there were a textbook example of what not to do, it is AUKUS.” Six months later, independent MP Monique Ryan asserted of AUKUS that “transparency and accountability… key to the social licence for any significant government endeavour… are sadly lacking.”

It is politically significant that support for greater public scrutiny comes not only from independent senator David Pocock, an AUKUS sceptic, but also from One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts, an AUKUS supporter. Debating the defence committee legislation in February 2026, Pocock asserted:

Public trust is not built through secrecy or enforced consensus; it’s built when Australians know that the right questions are being asked by people who are not constrained by party discipline or political self-protection. There are times when information must remain classified. This bill rightly recognises that. But secrecy in the national interest is not the same thing as secrecy for political convenience.
In the same debate, Roberts said:

There’s a perception amongst the public that the submarine deal associated with AUKUS is simply too much money at a time when the public are struggling… Having representatives from every parliamentary party will ensure that all political opinions are represented on the committee and that witness lists and inquiries conducted by the committee reflect a diversity of perspectives.

By invoking the same principle — accountability — Pocock and Roberts give us a clue to the surging support for One Nation. Roberts says that unity among the major parties “is making the public feel that they’re just not being listened to.” Is there a better example of this than the major parties’ handling of defence? •
